en.title: Laika's Wildwood Bravely Tackles Death, Earning Its PG-13 Rating
en.summary: Laika's latest stop-motion marvel, **Wildwood**, dares to explore mature themes of grief and loss, setting a new precedent for the studio's family-friendly fare. This visually stunning adventure proves that even younger audiences can handle complex emotional narratives.
en.body:
Laika has always pushed the boundaries of stop-motion animation, crafting worlds that are as intricate as they are imaginative. With their latest film, **Wildwood**, director **Travis Knight** and the studio have taken another significant leap, not just in visual artistry but in thematic depth. This ambitious adaptation of the children's book series is the first in Laika's feature filmography to earn a PG-13 rating, a decision that signals a profound trust in audiences, young and old, to engage with challenging subject matter.


The film centers on **Prue McKeel**, a determined young girl whose life is upended when her younger brother is snatched by a murder of crows and taken into the mysterious Impassable Wilderness. What follows is a breathtaking, albeit intense, journey into a magical parallel world. Here, Prue, aided by her classmate **Curtis**, discovers a land under siege by **Alexandra**, a grieving dowager governess. Alexandra's descent into dark magic, fueled by the tragic loss of her son and husband, creates a compelling, complex antagonist. The film unflinchingly depicts the consequences of grief, touching upon themes of death, loss, and vengeance in a way that resonates deeply, even within a fantastical setting.

> "Wildwood, even more than the book on which it's based, is unflinching in its depiction of death..."

## A Bold Narrative for a New Generation

For years, animated films aimed at younger audiences often tiptoed around the stark realities of mortality. **Wildwood**, however, embraces these darker elements head-on. While it imparts essential lessons about listening to parents and courage, it doesn't shy away from brushes with death and the profound impact of grief. This mature approach to storytelling, reminiscent of classic 80s adventure films and the works of **Don Bluth**, allows **Wildwood** to feel both nostalgic and refreshingly contemporary. The PG-13 rating isn't just a label; it's an acknowledgment that complex emotional arcs, even those involving peril and loss, can be vital to a story's power and resonance for young viewers.

## Why This Matters to Laika Fans

Laika's dedicated fanbase has come to expect a certain level of craftsmanship and emotional intelligence from their films, from **Coraline** to **Kubo and the Two Strings**. **Wildwood**’s willingness to tackle mature themes like death and grief head-on is precisely the kind of bold storytelling that distinguishes the studio. It signals a commitment to not talking down to audiences, trusting them to navigate complex narratives and emerge with a deeper understanding of emotional resilience. The film’s intricate stop-motion animation, combined with its unflinching portrayal of loss and the fight against despair, offers a rich tapestry that longtime fans will undoubtedly appreciate, while also potentially attracting new viewers drawn to its mature storytelling.

## What's Next

**Wildwood** opened in theaters on October 23, 2026. Audiences can now experience **Travis Knight**'s latest vision and witness firsthand how Laika continues to redefine animated storytelling.

content_raw: Laika’s new film Wildwood is the culmination of years of dedicated craftsmanship, pushing the boundaries of stop-motion animation to create something truly dazzling. For all its technical innovations, the animated film also harkens back to older movies, including the films of Don Bluth and the action-adventure sagas that were regular family fare in the 1980s. Wildwood is the first of Laika’s feature films to earn a PG-13 rating, but director Travis Knight and the studio trust audiences to handle its darker themes.  While Wildwood has kid-friendly lessons like “listen to your parents,” it also has some more grown-up brushes with death, grief, and control. Two kids, Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) and Curtis (Jacob Tremblay), embark on a mission to save Prue’s younger brother from a murder of crows, and they discover a parallel magical world under siege by a grieving dowager governess, Alexandra (Carey Mulligan). Her son died in a tragic horse-riding accident, and her husband followed in death from grief soon after. Desperate to reclaim just a little of the love she lost, Alexandra used dark magic to conjure her son’s spirit back into an automaton, but unhappy in his new mechanical shell, the contraption jumped out of their mansion, revealing to the townsfolk what she had done. Banished for using dark magic, the grief-stricken mother now plans to destroy the forest and displace its indigenous residents to look for her son’s lost remains.  In their mission to foil the dowager governess, both Prue and Curtis face loss and the chance to be brave to help one another. Curtis, a talkative nervous classmate who tries to chat with Prue about the games he plays, is the first to step up to give her time to escape the coyotes chasing after them. He’s captured and manipulated by Alexandra to join her ranks; later in battle, he loses one of his closest allies in this realm. Prue also experiences loss firsthand as one of the magical beings that helps her escape is shot down by an arrow. The camera doesn’t cut away from the cost of war or spare their fuzzy or feathered friends by then bringing them back magically to life once order is restored. There is a genuine sense of the finality of death.  In the 1980s, movies made for all age audiences, or even those directed at children, weren’t just about the Carebears. Many of them, both animated and live-action movies, also wrestled with loss like Wildwood , an aspect that’s missing from many present-day family-friendly movies which are sanitized to be as inoffensive as possible.
